sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As multimodal resources are transformed into media outputs, agentic AI is expected to stay aligned with design intent over long horizons. Designers follow briefs specifying goals, constraints, and deliverables, with later work building on earlier decisions. Recent work reuses design experience across tasks, yet alignment among artifacts within one project remains challenging. Agents therefore need to preserve and apply this intent across domains and as projects grow. We introduce Design Anything, a graph-based harness that preserves design intent outside the model and binds deliverables to the workflow steps that produce them through an intent-execution graph. A task contract retains constraints and decisions, selected designs become explicit inputs to later generations, and a deterministic controller uses bindings and execution records to check output types and counts, identify outstanding deliverables, and guide subsequent turns. We also introduce DesignAnything-Bench, with 228 tasks across 19 design domains, including 38 project families at scales of 6, 14, and 24 artifacts. With the LLM held fixed, Design Anything satisfies 85.0% and 92.5% of the brief's factual constraints with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash High and GPT-5.6 Sol High, respectively, exceeding the strongest same-model baselines by 15.4% and 14.4%. These gains reach 25.1% and 23.0% on 24-artifact tasks. Under each model, Design Anything leads or ties in constraint satisfaction in 18 of 19 domains. Professional designers also prefer its complete deliverable sets over those of same-model baselines in a blind evaluation.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Human design activity often begins with specific need, such as developing product, staging an exhibition, or building brand. Designers work from design brief, which states the initial design intent: the projects goals, constraints, and required deliverables. Such projects usually call for set of coordinated artifacts, including concept images, renderings, specification documents, videos, and slide decks, and later work builds on earlier design decisions, such as the selected concept and references (Gero, 1990; Gero and Kannengiesser, 2004; Dorst and Cross, 2001). Generative models and design tools can now produce individual artifacts (OpenAI, 2026; ByteDance Seed, 2026; Tripo, 2026; Zheng et al., 2025; Ge et al., 2025). Recent work on agentic artifact creation highlights the challenge of preserving requirements and earlier decisions throughout multi-step production (Wang et al., 2026). Long-horizon tasks remain difficult (Kwa et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b; Xie et al., 2024). Models do not reliably use the information in long contexts (Liu et al., 2024a; Hong et al., 2025), perform worse when requirements arrive over multiple turns (Laban et al., 2026), and, in long tool-use runs, stop too early, verify too little, and lose constraints (Yuan et al., 2026; Merrill et al., 2026). Staying aligned with design intent means delivering every requested artifact, meeting each constraint in every artifact it concerns, and carrying earlier design decisions forward so that the artifacts stay consistent; all three become harder as deliverables multiply. An agents performance depends not only on its large language model (LLM) but also on its harness, the software layer that manages tool calls, context, and multi-step execution (Yao et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024; Agashe et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026). Existing studies have explored harness mechanisms for sustained execution, including persistent requirement records and independent review of completion status (Ma et al., 2026), as well as canvases that organize artifacts and their reference relationships (Lin et al., 2026). Other studies reuse design experience accumulated over earlier tasks (Luo et al., 2026). These approaches either rely on model to judge whether the work is complete or check one artifact at time. Graph-based agent orchestration, recently discussed as graph engineering, makes task dependencies and execution state explicit (Kim et al., 2024; Wei, 2026; Feng et al., 2026). For long-horizon design, the challenge for harness is to ensure that recorded constraints and design 2 decisions continue to guide artifact production and to reliably identify unfinished deliverables. Therefore, this raises natural question: how can agentic AI consistently align with design intent over long-horizon tasks? To this end, we propose Design Anything, graph-based harness for long-horizon agentic design whose key idea is to keep design intent outside the model, in an explicit state the harness can check, and to bind each deliverable to the workflow steps that produce it; we call this state the intentexecution graph (Figure 3). persistent task contract records the deliverables, constraints, and design decisions made during the run, so later turns still see them. When later artifact builds on selected concept or supplied reference, the agent links it into the graph as an explicit input, so the artifact is generated from it rather than from fresh description (Figure 14). After each turn, deterministic controller uses the bindings, the execution records, and checks on output kind and count to find the outstanding deliverables, and starts another turn that names them; run succeeds only when none remain. The same configuration serves every domain (Figure 2; Appendix E). Evaluating such harness requires suitable benchmark. Some existing benchmarks include professional tasks with several deliverables (Sun et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b), among them design and creative tasks (Li et al., 2026b); others focus on workflow construction, tool planning, UI reproduction, poster generation, or single-image quality (Xue et al., 2025; Ki et al., 2025; Jeong et al., 2026; Si et al., 2025; Pang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). However, results at one project scale, the number of requested artifacts, do not show whether an agent stays aligned with design intent as the same project grows. We introduce DesignAnything-Bench for this purpose, with 228 tasks across 19 design domains, including 38 project families each posed at 6, 14, and 24 requested artifacts with shared background and inputs. Design Anything satisfies 85.0% of the briefs factual constraints (such as names and dimensions) with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash High and 92.5% with GPT-5.6 Sol High. Against the strongest baseline on the same LLM, it leads by 15.4% and 14.4% over all tasks and by 25.1% and 23.0% on 24-artifact tasks (Figure 1), and it leads or ties in 18 of 19 domains under each model (Figure 5). In blind evaluation of complete output sets by professional designers, the two Design Anything configurations receive the two highest estimated preference scores among the five configurations. Our contributions are threefold: Design Anything Harness. We propose Design Anything, harness that keeps design intent outside the model in an intentexecution graph binding each deliverable to the workflow steps that produce it. DesignAnything-Bench. We introduce DesignAnything-Bench, 228-task benchmark spanning 19 design domains, with 38 project families scaled from 6 to 24 artifacts, to test whether agents stay aligned with design intent across domains and as projects grow. Evaluation. With the LLM fixed, Design Anything satisfies more constraints than the strongest baseline overall and at every project scale, leads or ties in 18 of 19 domains, and receives the highest designer preference.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: Design Anything keeps design intent in an explicit state outside the model and operates on it with two loops (Figure 3). After formalizing what alignment with design intent requires of run (❶), we describe this state, the intentexecution graph (❷), which binds each deliverable to the workflow steps that produce it. The agent loop (❸) builds and executes this graph, and the delivery loop (❹) checks it to find unfinished deliverables and decide the next action.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: Holding the LLM fixed, we ask: (1) Can one harness fulfill briefs across domains (Anything)? (2) Can it do so as projects require more artifacts (At Scale)? (3) How does the full harness compare with reduced configurations in delivery and efficiency? We also ask which delivered sets professional designers prefer.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Task composition
sections.content: The benchmark spans 19 design domains with 12 tasks each (Figure 4). Tasks supply English briefs, input materials, and delivery requirements. For matched-scale comparisons, 38 project families share background and inputs across 6-, 14-, and 24-artifact versions (114 tasks). The 57 reference-material tasks test matching supplied objects; 57 breadth tasks add subjects and audiences. Each of these independent projects requests 6 or 14 artifacts. In total, 228 tasks represent 152 distinct projects (Appendix B.1). 5 Figure 4 DesignAnything-Bench contains 228 tasks across 19 domains. In (b), the inner ring shows task conditions; the outer ring shows requested artifact counts. Only matched-scale tasks reuse the same 38 families across scales; each other task is an independent project at one scale. Artifact count measures scale.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Evaluation measures
sections.content: In our work, delivery completion, constraint satisfaction, and cross-artifact consistency measure observable aspects of alignment in exported artifacts. Automatic evaluation follows Agent-as-a-Judge (Zhuge et al., 2025) (Appendix Table 3). Requirement fulfillment measures how well outputs meet the brief. Delivery completion is the share of requested files delivered, capped per category. Constraint satisfaction is the share of applicable factual constraints satisfied in every eligible artifact. For illustration, delivering three requested posters gives 100% delivery, but name required on all three and correct on only two fails that constraint. Table 1 pools satisfied constraints, not fully successful tasks. Reference fidelity measures the share of outputreference pairs depicting the same object (Appendix B.3). Cross-artifact consistency measures agreement among outputs. Identity consistency compares outputs with designated output from the same run (the anchor), measuring the share of pairs depicting the same object. Reference fidelity instead uses supplied asset. Set consistency scores shared visual rules, such as palette and typography, on 100-point rubric. Design quality (100-point scale) covers technical quality, aesthetics, text rendering, and domain criteria (Li et al., 2026a). Aggregate image-checklist means are multiplied by aggregate delivery completion, reflecting both image quality and missing work (Appendix B.3). vision-language judge scores the checklists; Appendix B.4 documents calibration of the other automatic judges against human annotations. Designer preference asks professional designers which delivered set they would hand to the client, comparing outputs for the same brief without seeing system names and allowing ties. Table 1 summarizes these choices using BradleyTerry estimates (Section 3.5).

sections.title: 3.3.1 Overall and cross-domain results
sections.content: Overall comparison. Across 228 tasks in 19 domains  (Table 1)  , Design Anything leads each LLM group on constraint satisfaction (85.0% on DeepSeek; 92.5% on GPT), reference fidelity, and identity consistency. OpenDesign and Codex score higher on set consistency; Codex also has higher point estimates for delivery, technical quality, and text rendering. JarvisHub leaves 12.4% of artifacts undelivered. Design Anythings strengths thus lie in satisfying constraints and preserving object identity across outputs, one aspect of carrying design decisions forward. Appendix C.5 examines reference reuse and its association with identity consistency within JarvisHub. Cross-domain results. Figure 5 tests how widely this advantage extends across the 19 domains, with 12 tasks per domain. Design Anything leads or ties in 18 under each LLM. JarvisHub leads in product design on DeepSeek, and Codex in exhibition design on GPT. This broad coverage supports Anything: our method fulfills constraints across diverse design domains. sections.title: 3.3.2 Results at scale
sections.content: To test At Scale, Figure 7 compares five configurations on 38 matched project families at 6, 14, and 24 artifacts. At 24, Design Anything achieves 85.7% constraint satisfaction on DeepSeek and 91.9% on GPT, leading OpenDesign by 25.1% and Codex by 23.0%. The constraint-satisfaction advantage thus persists as the same projects require more artifacts. Figure 7 Design Anything retains its constraint-satisfaction advantage from 6 to 24 artifacts. Panels show (a) delivery completion and (b) constraint satisfaction on 38 matched families. Solid lines with filled markers denote DS; dashed lines with hollow markers denote GPT. Design Anythings advantage at larger scales lies in satisfying the briefs constraints throughout the delivered 8 set. On 24-artifact tasks, Codex delivers over 97% of requested artifacts but satisfies 68.9% of constraints, compared with 91.9% for Design Anything using the same LLM. Each constraint counts as satisfied only when it holds in every eligible artifact, so this gap reflects more reliable fulfillment across the set, beyond delivering the requested files. Paired bootstrap comparisons and sensitivity checks for missing deliveries support this conclusion (Appendix C.4). Figure 8 illustrates how the outputs expand across three matched architectural design tasks, from spatial views and drawings to shading details, documents, and video. Figure 8 Design Anything (GPT-5.6 Sol High) on RIVER COMMONS with 6, 14, and 24 requested artifacts. Stacks denote documents; play icons denote videos. Counts give credited artifacts.

sections.title: 3.5 Human evaluation
sections.content: To assess the delivered sets from professional design perspective, twelve designers in five disciplines compare outputs on 185 tasks, yielding 1,019 blind pairwise judgments. They choose which set they would hand to the client, with ties allowed. Design Anything is preferred over each baseline using the same LLM: designers choose it in 82% of judgments against OpenDesign, 70% against Codex, and 51% against JarvisHub, compared with 37% for JarvisHub and 12% ties (Figure 9b). Figure 9 The two Design Anything configurations have the highest estimated designer preference. (a) BradleyTerry estimates with 95% task-and-designer bootstrap intervals (1,019 judgments, 185 tasks, 12 designers). (b) Pairwise choices with ties; counts judgments. DA denotes Design Anything; the bold last row compares its DeepSeek and GPT configurations. Our GPT and DeepSeek configurations rank first and second in estimated designer preference (74.0% and 60.7%), both with 95% intervals above 50% (Figure 9a). These BradleyTerry estimates average each configurations fitted preference probabilities against the other four; direct comparisons between our two configurations connect the LLM groups. The pairwise choices and joint ranking show that designers more often select Design Anythings delivered sets for client handoff, complementing the automatic measures with professional judgment of the project as whole. Appendix B.5 gives the evaluation and estimation details.

sections.title: 4 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Design Anything, harness that keeps design intent outside the model in an intentexecution graph, which binds each deliverable to the workflow steps that produce it, and DesignAnything-Bench, 228 10 long-horizon design tasks across 19 domains and three project scales. With the LLM fixed, Design Anything satisfies more of the briefs constraints than the strongest baseline overall and at every project scale, leads or ties in 18 of 19 domains, and receives the highest designer preference. In the study of the delivery loop (Section 3.4), the full harness delivers nearly as many artifacts as harness that answers every stop with generic prompt to keep working, at about one-third of its LLM cost. Limitations are discussed in Appendix F.

sections.title: A Implementation and Runtime Details
sections.content: A.1 Task contract The task contract, the intent layer of the intentexecution graph, is stored as structured project object visible on the canvas. It holds the final deliverable description, stable deliverable identifiers, public success criteria, constraints, decisions marked as coming from the user or the agent, and open questions. It holds no execution phase or completion counter, so revising it updates intent rather than recording progress. A.2 Graph construction and artifact ownership The binding β is implemented through delivery groups, named sets of nodes. Graph-building operations accept typed node descriptions, configurations, connections, and the delivery group that receives them. They can create new nodes or associate eligible existing nodes with that group. Groups explicitly declare which contract deliverables they implement; an empty declaration denotes supporting work. Shared groups require output ownership information so that an artifact for one deliverable is not automatically counted toward another. Dependency declarations and port-level edges serve different purposes: the former express ordering between groups, while the latter carry concrete inputs to operations. A.3 Operational delivery checks For each deliverable, the controller finds its bound nodes through the delivery groups that claim it and through node ownership, and examines the status of the bound executable nodes; data-only inputs and annotations do not count as artifact-generating execution. In groups shared by several deliverables, an execution failure that cannot be attributed to one item remains group-level failure signal rather than being assigned to an item. Output-form checks use node capability declarations. An image-producing operation cannot satisfy readabledocument deliverable merely because its image resembles document, and minimum-page declaration requires an implementation capable of paginated output without verifying the realized page count. Quantity checks count supported output items rather than generation nodes. The benchmarks artifact evaluation is therefore necessary even when every bound node has finished. A.4 Observation and new turns The state summary is compact projection of workflow state regenerated between turns; detailed read tools expose individual nodes, connections, configurations, and outputs. After turn ends, the controller reads the workflow graph and the execution records and lists obligations for the root goal, deliverables, decisions, required questions, and execution. Each obligation is open, waiting, in progress, satisfied, failed, or cancelled. The controller then selects the next action in this order: 1. Stop on cancellation, loss of edit access, execution failures, or repeated-error limit. 2. Wait if turn, job, or delegated execution is still active, or if decision requested from the user is still pending. 3. Terminate unsuccessfully on failed obligations, or successfully when the root obligation is satisfied and no unresolved obligation remains. The root obligation is derived, not declared: it is satisfied only when every deliverable is delivered and no required question, pending decision, or running execution remains. 4. For remaining work, check progress and resource limits; either start another model turn or stop with an explicit reason. The message starting new turn names the outstanding deliverables and, for each, the blocking reason, such as missing output form or quantity shortfall. The model then decides whether to read state, modify contract, build or edit graph, execute an operation, delegate work, or request decision. Progress monitoring separates obligation changes from observable workflow changes. Repeatedly restating plan is not sufficient evidence of artifact progress. Progress limits stop repeated new turns that make no 15 progress, while allowing active execution and pending decisions; the thresholds and run limits are listed in Appendix C.1. A.5 Automatic verifier When every deliverable is delivered, an automatic verifier reviews the workflow graph in the background: deterministic checks first list structural problems, such as unconnected nodes, and the verifier checks them against the success criteria and returns concrete findings to the agent. Visual design critique is available only as tool the agent may call. Goal completion remains governed by the control layer. The verifier is enabled in the main comparison and the Complete delivery-loop configuration, and disabled in the two reduced delivery-loop configurations and all planning configurations. Recorded run settings are in Appendix C.1; component-study configurations are in Appendix D.

sections.title: B Benchmark Construction and Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: This appendix describes task construction, output processing, metric definitions, judge calibration, and the designer study. Complete results and sensitivity analyses are in Appendix C; controlled component studies and visual evidence follow in Appendices and E. B.1 Task construction and benchmark independence The 19 domains are product design; vehicle styling; furniture and home products; architecture; interior design; exhibition design; landscape design; fashion and textiles; jewelry and accessories; brand identity; graphic design and advertising; books and illustration; packaging; UI/UX; information design and data visualization; animation and storyboarding; game art and worldbuilding; e-commerce product imagery; and advertising and fashion photography. Figure 4 summarizes their equal representation. The task counts below distinguish scale variants from distinct project identities. Task condition Tasks/domain Tasks by artifact count Total tasks Projects Matched scales Reference materials Breadth Total 2 3 = 6 3 3 12 38 26 19 83 14 38 31 38 107 38 0 0 38 114 57 57 228 38 57 57 Each domain contributes two base project families: one asks the system to propose alternatives and select one, and the other fixes the direction in the brief. Each family has three scale versions with shared background and inputs, yielding 19 2 3 = 114 tasks. Only the 14and 24-artifact versions request process artifacts, such as alternative directions and specifications. The three reference-material and three breadth projects per domain are independent projects, adding 114 tasks. Each requests either 6 or 14 artifacts, with no additional scale variants of the same project. Thus 19 (2 3 + 3 + 3) = 228 tasks correspond to 19 (2 + 3 + 3) = 152 project identities. Only the base tasks support within-family scale comparisons. Evaluation specifications. Each specification translates the public brief and supplied materials into scoring criteria. Requested categories specify expected quantities, mark core categories, and distinguish process from final deliverables. Additional rules specify factual constraints, source and target artifacts for comparisons, and when criterion is inapplicable. Systems receive only the English brief and materials. Benchmark independence. Tasks were authored with LLM assistance from per-domain topic plan and reviewed by the authors, with English scenarios as the only system input. No internal label of Design Anything enters scoring. During development, Design Anything was run on separate 20-task pilot corpus and on small subsets of the final corpus (5-task subsets and 13 base-scale tasks) to fix infrastructure failures. No brief was revised in response to any systems score except under recorded defect rule applied identically to all systems. 16 Each system kept whatever general-purpose skills its product bundles; none used skills written for particular design domain, which could supply prebuilt design procedures, and none received task-specific hints. Execution and scoring use frozen task specifications, and each run is scored against the specification of the brief it received. The three tasks of one book project family (6, 14, and 24 artifacts) exist in two versions: OpenDesign and JarvisHub received the earlier archival photography brief, while both Design Anything configurations and Codex received the later historical astronomy plate brief; the other 225 tasks have identical briefs and specifications for all systems. B.2 Output processing and assignment The evaluator consumes package of delivered files and evaluation specifications, independent of the systems internal representation. It can therefore compare canvas-based workflow with file-based agent without requiring the latter to reconstruct canvas. Import records distinguish supplied inputs, primary deliverables, and derived representations. Multiple file formats of the same work are associated to avoid counting preview and its source as two deliveries. Input materials copied into an output directory remain inputs, identified by their content. HTML decks are rendered by their own page structure, and PDF and presentation files keep their page and text information; file whose pages cannot be read makes page minimum unmeasurable rather than failed. Rendered deck pages can be inspected for consistency but do not count as separately requested artifacts. To assign images to requested categories, the classifier scores each category and an unassigned option for every image; the assignment fills each category up to its expected quantity and uses each image at most once. Remaining images may be recorded as overflow without raising completion above the expected quantity. This matching uses the artifact and the specification, not Design Anything node labels, group names, or execution order. The classifier and evaluator versions are given in Appendix C, and the classifiers calibration in Appendix B.4. On the 100-point scale, the set-consistency judge scores Design Anything 9.2 points below the designers, while it scores JarvisHub 1.6 and OpenDesign 2.0 points above them. Neither judges error favors Design Anything. 19 Category assignment. The classifier assigns delivered artifacts to the requested categories used to compute delivery completion. Calibration covers 120 tasks. Human-human agreement is Cohens κ = 0.89; humanclassifier agreement is κ = 0.83, using the two annotators consensus labels as the reference. Text transcription. For text transcription used in constraint checks, human-human agreement is Cohens κ = 0.98. Human-machine agreement is κ = 0.92 on the subset where the two annotators agree, using their consensus annotations as the reference. B.5 Designer evaluation protocol Participants and assignment. The designer study (Section 3.5) uses the same run of each system that the automatic measures score, so no run is selected by appearance. Twelve designers rate 185 tasks in five discipline groups: visual communication (four designers; brand identity, graphic design and advertising, packaging, books and illustration, information design, photography, and e-commerce imagery), digital interaction (two; UI/UX, game art, animation and storyboarding), product (two; product design, vehicle styling, furniture), spatial (two; architecture, interior, exhibition, and landscape design), and fashion and accessories (two). Within group, tasks are stratified by domain, task condition, and project scale and dealt to designers in rotation; each designer first rates three warm-up tasks, and some tasks are rated second time by another designer of the group. Pairings and displayed evidence. Baseline comparisons pair systems within an LLM: Design Anything, OpenDesign, and JarvisHub pairwise on DeepSeek, and Design Anything against Codex on GPT; Design Anything on DeepSeek is also compared directly with Design Anything on GPT, which connects the two model groups on one BradleyTerry scale. Each comparison shows every file the evaluator assigned to requested category, in the briefs deliverable order. Whole-set judgments and estimation. Designers see the brief with reference translation, never system names, reasoning, or completion claims. Sides are randomized. They choose the set they would rather hand to the client, answering left, right, or approximately equal. The study yielded 1,019 whole-set judgments, which support the results in Section 3.5. Whole-set preference is estimated with BradleyTerry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952), Pr(i j) = eβi /(eβi + eβj ), fitted to the 1,019 judgments. tie contributes half win to each side. For each of the five configurations, we average its fitted preference probabilities against the other four, weighting opponents equally regardless of the number of observed comparisons. This is the probability of beating uniformly sampled other configuration, not raw head-to-head win fraction. We report 95% intervals from 2,000 bootstrap replicates over tasks and designers.

sections.title: D Ablation Studies
sections.content: The studies below examine the delivery loop, planning interfaces, and state summaries. In the delivery-loop study, Stop at model end versus Generic prompt tests prompting after normal stop within the same reduced harness; Generic prompt versus Complete compares bundle of mechanisms and its execution efficiency. The planning and state-summary studies examine narrower changes separately. The delivery-loop study uses 19 tasks from the main corpus; planning and state-summary studies use separate tasks and harness versions. Each study reports its own configuration and contributes no observations to the 228-task benchmark aggregates. No study uses skills written for particular design domain. D.1 Delivery loop and execution efficiency This study asks whether replying after the model stops restores delivery, and how the complete harness changes repeated generation and cost. It uses the 24-artifact version of one base family per domain (19 tasks), the family whose brief asks the system to propose alternative directions and select one, with the LLM and image-generation configuration of the main comparison. Each configuration has one run per task, including fresh Complete run separate from the main comparison. The verifier is enabled for Complete and disabled for the two reduced configurations. All three are scored with the same evaluator. Approval requests raised through the checkpoint tool receive the same scripted answers in every configuration; question written into final message ends the turn, and Stop at model end provides no reply. Table 14 Delivery-loop configurations. The first two configurations differ only in generic reply after stopping within the reduced harness. Complete restores the full set of mechanisms. Mechanism Stop at model end Generic prompt Complete After the model stops End run Removed Contract and planning tools Removed Task and progress reminders Automatic verifier Disabled Batched asynchronous execution Removed Fixed prompt to keep working Removed Removed Disabled Removed Delivery loop (Section 2.4) Retained Retained Enabled Retained Configuration definitions. Stop at model end removes the delivery-loop controller, the contract and planning tools, batched asynchronous execution, and every channel that restates the task or its progress, such as reminders of the original brief and progress lines in the status message. Synchronous execution, read tools, context compaction, scripted approval answers, and retries after transport failures remain, since generic tool-using harness has them. run ends when the model ends turn without calling tool. Generic prompt keeps every removal and, whenever the model ends turn, sends the fixed user message Continue working until everything the original brief asks for is fully delivered. If everything is already delivered, say so briefly and make no canvas changes. The message names no outstanding item. The loop stops after two consecutive rounds without canvas change, after 100 turns, or at the 150-minute wall-clock limit. Complete is the full harness of Section 2. Stop at model end versus Generic prompt tests the addition of the fixed prompt; Generic prompt versus Complete compares the combined mechanisms in Table 14. Delivery and constraint outcomes. Table 2 compares three configurations on the 19 paired 24-artifact tasks. Complete achieves 96.1% delivery and 90.4% constraint satisfaction. It improves both over Stop at model end (p = 0.018 and = 0.001), but its delivery and constraint differences from Generic prompt are not statistically significant (p = 0.39 and = 0.063). This supports fulfillment gains over stopping unaided on larger projects; the comparison with Generic prompt does not isolate one component. Paired tests are two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests paired by task; tasks with equal values are excluded and tied absolute differences receive average ranks. Against the complete harness, Stop at model end delivers less on 8 tasks and more on 3 and satisfies fewer constraints on 11 tasks and more on none. Generic prompt delivers more on 7 tasks and less on 4, with 8 ties; constraint satisfaction favors Complete on 6 tasks and Generic prompt on 1. Early stops and constraint outcomes. The Runs < 50% column counts runs delivering fewer than half of their requested artifacts. Six Stop at model end runs fall below half delivery against no Complete run (Fisher exact test, two-sided = 0.020, one-sided = 0.010). All six end within three turns: three ask for confirmation of direction or costly next stage, two announce further deliverables, and one exhausts the output-token limit before building anything. Generic prompt recovers each to 23 or 24 deliverables. Missing deliveries explain only part of the constraint gap. Constraints on wholly undelivered categories count as unsatisfied (Appendix B.3); these six runs account for at most 12 of the 24 fewer constraints satisfied relative to Complete. At least 12 fewer satisfied constraints therefore occur in runs that deliver 20 or more of their 24 artifacts. Repeated generation. On the same 19 tasks  (Table 2)  , the generic configuration issues more generation requests than the complete harness on 15 tasks and fewer on 3 (p = 0.002); counting only completed requests gives 14 and 3 (p = 0.001). The extra requests come after the deliverables are largely in place, when the prompt keeps the agent regenerating delivered work; in one task the generic configuration issues 68 requests against 27. D.2 Planning-interface study This study asks whether structured planning interfaces improve delivery when other channels for tracking requirements remain available. It compares three planning interfaces. Structured retains the structured project-plan and workflow-construction tools. Text plan replaces those tools with an instruction to maintain free-text deliverable checklist. Planning tools off removes them without replacement instruction. Delivery groups, outstanding-work messages, direct canvas reads, status tools, retained history, and new model turns remain available in every configuration. The automatic verifier is disabled in all three configurations, including Structured, to keep its availability fixed. On eight tasks, delivery completion is 7.7 points lower with Planning tools off than with Structured, and 2.1 points lower with Text plan. These comparisons measure the incremental contribution of structured planning interfaces alongside the other channels for tracking the task. Those retained channels offer possible explanation for the modest gaps. D.3 State-summary efficiency The state-summary study tests whether the summary reduces direct inspection of the canvas. It removes the summary while retaining direct read tools and measures the fraction of tool calls devoted to active canvas 29 reading. Nine of ten paired tasks read more without the summary; the geometric mean ratio of reading fractions is 2.06 (one-sided exact sign test, = 0.011). The paired result shows larger share of tool calls devoted to direct state inspection without the summary; the experiment does not measure final design quality.

sections.title: F Limitations
sections.content: Evaluation and run variability. Each configuration contributes one final result per task; repeated runs would further characterize run-to-run variation. The image-checklist component of design quality relies on vision-language judge. Whole-set designer preferences complement these measurements without identifying which properties drive preference. Scope of system comparisons. The main comparisons hold the LLM fixed and evaluate complete systems, including their tools and execution policies. The delivery-loop comparison bundles several mechanisms; planning-interface and state-summary studies examine narrower changes within their own configurations (Appendix D). Runtime checks and design intent. The model chooses the bindings between deliverables and workflow steps. The controller checks their execution, output forms, and quantities, but cannot determine whether bound artifact is the one the brief requested or whether its content satisfies the constraints. Artifact evaluation remains necessary. Task and interaction coverage. The benchmark uses English briefs and scripted client for checkpoint questions. For fair comparison, it includes only modalities that every compared system can generate: Design Anything also generates 3D meshes and audio (grey in Figure 3), but not all compared systems do. We leave these modalities, other languages, and live client feedback to future evaluations.
